newsitem.title: USA: McKinney wins re-election in nasty Georgia race.
newsitem.headline: McKinney wins re-election in nasty Georgia race.

text.p: U.S. Representative Cynthia McKinney claimed victory in Tuesday's election, but her angrily contested campaign against Republican John Mitnick showed no sign of shedding its propensity for racial invective.

Long after midnight, when she was about seven points ahead of Mitnick, the 41-year-old liberal appeared among her supporters in the role of the first black woman from the South to be elected to Congress by a white-majority district.

"Finally, a train called history has pulled into our station. And while some of you thought it might never come, just remember this is America, a place where hope is our common currency and justice is our creed," McKinney said.
With 73 pct of precincts reporting, local news reports at about 2 a.m. EST put Mckinney's support at 57.9 percent against 42.1 percent for Mitnick.

McKinney became the first Georgia black woman to be elected to Congress in 1992 from the former black-majority 11th district that snaked more than 200 miles from surburban Atlanta to Savannah, Georgia.
Last year, however, the Supreme Court ruled her district unconstitutional and Georgia's voting districts were redrawn, leaving her with the new 4th district, which is more than 60 percent white.
But with only a seven percentage-point margin separating the two candidates, the news of her victory came as a bombshell to her opponent, who had led McKinney by a wide margin early in the evening.
"I don't know on what basis she's doing that. I see no basis to declare a victor on either side," Mitnick said.

Mitnick, who is Jewish, had tried to sway voters against McKinney by underscoring her refusal to support a congressional resolution decrying the hate speech of an aide to Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan.
The controversy came to a head when McKinney's father, civil rights leader Billy McKinney, resigned from the campaign after referring to Mitnick in public as "a racist Jew."
"John Mitnick needs to work with me to set straight the damage he has done," McKinney told supporters, clearly laying the blame for race-baiting at her opponent's doorstep.
"John Mitnick attempted to paint me as a racist and an anti-Semite in order to divide the Democratic coalition and feed his own political ambitions."

Mitnick, who denied the allegation, said in a television interview he believed the election had been fraught with impropriety. He threatened to lodge a formal complaint if he found concrete evidence to support his suspicions.
